readerTitle: When more members make the club worse
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (서퍼클럽, 요리 커뮤니티 앱) + 실제 관찰 (Usenet의 'Eternal September') + 가상 적용 (프리랜서 마켓플레이스)
insight: 네트워크의 가치는 몇 명이 있느냐가 아니라 누가 들어오고, 공간과 주의력이 얼마나 남느냐로 정해진다. 성장이 가치를 깎는 순간이 있다.
misconception: 네트워크 효과가 있는 사업은 사람이 늘수록 언제나 더 좋아진다.

sources.text: The Jargon File, entry "September that never ended"
네트워크 경제학의 일반 개념 (부정적 네트워크 효과, 혼잡, 품질 희석)
서퍼클럽, 요리 앱, 프리랜서 마켓플레이스는 설명용 가상 사례이며 모든 수치는 가상

factChecks.note: Eternal September: 1993년 9월경 AOL이 회원에게 Usenet 접근을 열어 주면서 신규 유입이 끊이지 않게 되었다는 내용입니다. 정확한 시점과 표현을 Jargon File 등 1차 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도와 일반적 흐름만 적었습니다.
서퍼클럽 회원 40명 → 400명, 테이블 12석 → 60석 등은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: When more members make the club worse
body: A supper club grows from 40 members to 400. A cooking app grows from 2,000 users to 200,000.
Both owners celebrate. A year later, both are losing the members they cared about most. Growth didn't fail them. Growth *was* the problem.

image.label: A cozy dinner table next to an overcrowded one
image.brief: 좌우 분할 일러스트. 왼쪽은 8명이 둘러앉아 대화하는 아늑한 저녁 식탁, 오른쪽은 같은 공간에 사람이 빽빽해 접시와 팔꿈치가 부딪히는 식탁. 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your supper club has a waitlist.
body: You host monthly dinners where food lovers meet each other. Members say the best part is the conversation. Word has spread, and 300 people want in.
What do you do?

options.text: Let them all in and sell bigger events
options.feedback: You gain ticket sales fast, but you trade away the small tables and real conversations that made people want to join.

options.text: Keep each dinner small and add more dinners, grouped by interest
options.feedback: You grow without crowding each table. It costs more work and hosts, but it protects what members actually pay for.

options.text: Raise the price to slow the waitlist
options.feedback: Fewer people join, which eases crowding. But price filters for money, not for the guests your members want to meet.

cards.title: The supper club got crowded.
body: The owner chose growth. Dinners went from 12 seats to 60. Tables got loud. People talked only to the friends they came with.
The early regulars, the ones who brought great wine and stories, came less often. New members found a busy room of strangers. Each extra guest had made the dinner a little worse for everyone else.
This is **congestion**: a fixed space, table or resource shared by too many people.

cards.title: The cooking app got noisy.
body: The app's forum had no space limit. Its problem was different. As it grew, the same beginner questions appeared daily. Spam and recipe ads crept in.
Skilled home cooks, who once answered questions for fun, got tired of scrolling past noise. They posted less. Then the answers got worse, and beginners got less help too.
This is **dilution**: new members who don't match the network lower its quality for everyone.

image.label: An expert's answer buried under repeated posts
image.brief: 스마트폰 화면 속 커뮤니티 피드. 정성스러운 요리 답변 하나가 비슷한 질문 글과 광고 글 수십 개 아래에 묻혀 있음. 실제 앱 UI나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Negative network effects
body: A **negative network effect** is when each new member makes the product worse for existing members. It's the reverse of the usual story, where more people add more value.
Most networks have both forces at once. Early on, the good side wins. Past some point, crowding or noise can win instead. What matters is *who* joins and how much shared space or attention is left.

image.label: A value curve that rises, then bends down
image.brief: 가로축 "Members", 세로축 "Value to each member". 곡선이 올라가다가 정점 이후 꺾여 내려감. 정점 오른쪽에 "Congestion", "Dilution" 라벨.

cards.title: The September that never ended
body: Usenet was an early internet discussion network. Every September, a wave of new university students joined and broke its unwritten rules for a while, then learned them.

In 1993, AOL opened Usenet to its large base of users. The newcomers kept arriving, faster than the culture could absorb them. Long-time users called it the "Eternal September," and many moved elsewhere.
The network didn't shrink. It got bigger and, for its core members, worse.

cards.title: Don't fear growth. Manage it.
body: A small network that never reaches critical mass dies too. Gates and caps can stop you before you're big enough to be useful.
Fixes also cost something. Smaller tables need more hosts. Moderation needs people or tools. Entry rules can feel unwelcoming.
The goal is not to stay small. It's to grow in a way that adds the right members and keeps crowding and noise in check.

cards.title: Now it's a freelance marketplace.
body: Your platform connects small businesses with freelance designers. Designer sign-ups have tripled. Now each job gets 80 bids, many low-effort. Good designers win less often, and buyers are overwhelmed.
What's your move?

options.text: Keep adding designers. More supply is a network effect
options.feedback: More choice helps at first, but past a point it buries buyers in noise and pushes your best designers away.

options.text: Raise the bar to join and limit bids per job, showing the best matches first
options.feedback: You may slow sign-ups, but buyers see fewer, better bids and strong designers win enough work to stay.

options.text: Spend heavily to bring in more buyers
options.feedback: More jobs give designers more chances, which helps. But buyers still face 80 low-effort bids, so the noise remains.

cards.softwareNote: In software, dilution often shows up as spam, low-quality listings or flooded inboxes. Watch whether your most active users post, list or reply less as the network grows.

cards.title: Bigger helps only until it gets crowded or noisy.
body: Every network has a point where new members start taking value away. Watch what your best members do, not just how many members you have.
**Try it today:** name your three most valuable customers or members. Ask each one: has it gotten better or worse here since we grew?
